chapter: Armstrong, Parker and life inside the Basie band
title: Playing record solos versus new ones; Lester never repeated a solo
summary: Basie bandsmen would extend a hit solo; Lester Young would not repeat solos except on records.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Were the musicians kind of encouraged then to play the solos on their records?

Yeah, because they knew they was going to reach somebody out there that was going -- after a while, was going to be -- maybe hum it with them. So if -- maybe if Sweets did something that was -- that really caught on, well, Basie would feature him, maybe, on this particular tune and let him play six or seven choruses instead -- of course, on the record, it would only be like one chorus or something like that. But he'd let him play six or seven choruses and we'd find some riffs and nice harmony, licks and riffs and things to play under him and, of course, then the kids would enjoy that because they would be hearing something new. Then they would be hearing the original solo that they had -- you know, that they had really attracted their attention.
I can't imagine Lester ever playing -- repeating a solo. Did he ever?

Well, we had a hard time with Prez repeating solos except on the records, on the records, you know. Then, of course, like on the records, now, the longest solo he took on a record, I believe, was -- Lester Leaps In, when they featured him all like that. Of course, now the other things would be like new arrangements and he never played the same solo. You know, like -- only the records.
But only -- when we were doing the other tunes, he wouldn't play the same solo.
